Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Painter
  trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Emergency Contexts: Ambulances, Workplace: Workplace, Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones
  Threat: Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma

Vignette:
John is a 55-year-old African American man who has come to therapy after experiencing significant distress following the unexpected death of his brother. John and his brother were very close, sharing a deep bond that had sustained them through many life challenges. The trauma of losing his brother was compounded by the suddenness and unexpected nature of the event, leaving John with an overwhelming sense of grief and disorientation. The day of the incident, John had been working at his usual job as a painter when he received a call from one of his brother's friends informing him about the accident. The moment he heard the news, John felt his body tense up; it was as if every muscle in his frame prepared for some imminent threat. He left work immediately and rushed to the hospital where emergency vehicles were still present. The sight and sound of ambulances triggered a flood of emotions, making him feel an intense need to protect himself from further harm. Since that day, John has found it increasingly difficult to maintain his sense of safety. At night, he often lies awake, feeling particularly vulnerable in the darkness, convinced that danger could be lurking just beyond his line of sight. Even inside his own home, where he once felt secure, he remains on high alert, always poised and ready for any threat. John’s workplace has also become a source of anxiety. The sounds and sights associated with his job now remind him of the day he received the devastating news. He often finds himself pausing mid-task, overwhelmed by an intense but vague sense of grief that washes over him without clear visual memories to anchor it. These moments are particularly distressing because they leave John feeling disconnected from reality, as if he is living in a haze. John’s social life has also suffered significantly since the loss of his brother. Conversations about people losing loved ones now trigger intense emotional responses within him, making it challenging for him to engage with others on even basic topics. He avoids these conversations at all costs, which has led to increasing isolation from friends and colleagues. John feels that he doesn’t know himself anymore; the person who was once vibrant and engaged has been replaced by someone who is constantly vigilant and withdrawn. His wife, though supportive, finds it difficult to understand why simple daily interactions have become so challenging for him. They have grown distant as a result, with both of them feeling frustrated but unsure how to bridge the gap. John’s identity feels fragmented; he questions his sense of self and whether life can ever return to something resembling normalcy. John has come to therapy seeking help in navigating these overwhelming feelings. He is most afraid that he will never be able to move past this grief, and that the loss of his brother will continue to overshadow every aspect of his life. Despite his fears, John also hopes for a future where he can find some measure of peace and reclaim a sense of himself. Through our conversations, it has become clear that the unexpected death of John’s brother has fundamentally altered his perception of safety and self-worth. His symptoms are not just clinical labels but lived experiences that have shaped his daily functioning and relationships. The goal in therapy will be to help John process these emotions, rebuild a sense of identity, and gradually reconnect with life beyond the trauma.
